items.title: macOS-setup
items.text:
Files and scripts useful for setting up a new Mac. Helps keep synchronisation between my different Mac computers and offers a backup.

Set up a new Mac with

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eshwen/macOS-setup/main/bootstrap.sh | bash

Check out the docs by clicking the badge above.

items.title: See Also
items.text:
• Adding ssh keys to GitHub: https://help.github.com/en/enterprise/2.16/user/articles/generating-a-new-ssh-key-and-adding-it-to-the-ssh-agent
  • Emacs reference card: https://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/refcards/pdf/refcard.pdf
  • Sort all folders in Finder alphabetically: https://apple.stackexchange.com/questions/22717/how-to-set-arrange-by-for-all-the-folders-in-the-finder
  • Mac glyphs in unicode/HTML: https://apple.stackexchange.com/questions/55727/where-can-i-find-the-unicode-symbols-for-mac-functional-keys-command-shift-e

items.title: Installation
items.text:
Run the bootstrap script in the Terminal:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eshwen/macOS-setup/main/bootstrap.sh | bash

It goes through these steps, explaining each one and asking before running it, so you can skip any of them. It asks for your password the first time a step needs it:

  1. Installs Rosetta 2 (on Apple Silicon), Homebrew and the Xcode Command Line Tools
  2. Clones this repo into ~/GitHub/macOS-setup (set MACOS_SETUP_DIR to change this)
  3. Installs everything in the Brewfile
  4. Copies the fonts and system sounds, and installs Garamond Expert for LaTeX
  5. Applies the trackpad and Finder settings, and sets the Terminal profile
  6. Installs Oh My Zsh and its extensions, and turns them on

It's safe to re-run, e.g., after adding packages to the Brewfile. Steps that are already done are skipped without asking. If you've already cloned the repo, run ./bootstrap.sh from it instead.

To run every step without being asked, pass --yes:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eshwen/macOS-setup/main/bootstrap.sh | bash -s -- --yes

items.title: Manual steps
items.text:
Once it finishes,

  1. Log out and back in so the trackpad settings take effect
  2. Sign in to apps, and install the programs not available on Homebrew
  3. Set up verified Git commits

items.title: Time Machine
items.text:
Time Machine is a great backup utility, but it's not perfect. One of the drawbacks is that - from the GUI - it's not easy to create complex exclusions from the backup.

Since I do a lot of Python development, I don't want to back up virtual environments, etc. To exclude these, you can use find to search for the directories and pipe them to tmutil, e.g.,

find `pwd` -maxdepth 3 -type d -name '.venv' | xargs -n 1 tmutil addexclusion

to exclude the .venv directory.

items.title: System sounds
items.text:
I don't like some of the system sound effects in Big Sur. I've uploaded Basso and Glass from Catalina. bootstrap.sh copies them to ~/Library/Sounds. To do it by hand, run

mkdir ~/Library/Sounds
cp Basso_Catalina.aiff Glass_Catalina.aiff ~/Library/Sounds/

Then, in System Preferences Sound, they should be available.

items.title: Configuration options
items.text:
bootstrap.sh applies these settings. To change them by hand,

  • Enable 3-finger drag on the trackpad
    • Go to System Preferences Accessibility Pointer Control
    • Under Mouse & Trackpad Trackpad Options... select three finger drag from the dropdown menu and tick the checkbox
  • Order everything in every directory within Finder alphabetically
    • In the menu bar in Finder, go to View Show View Options
    • Ensure Group By and Sort By have the value Name and click Use As Defaults

items.title: Useful shortcuts
items.text:
• Forward delete: fn + ⌫
  • Show inspector (so Get Info shows for active file): ⌘ + ⌥ + i
  • Toggle to show/hide hidden files and directories (i.e., prefixed with .): ⌘ + ⇧ + .

items.title: Rosetta 2
items.text:
Rosetta 2 is Apple's utility to translate Intel-based (x86) apps, so they're Apple Silicon-compatible. It's no longer bundled with macOS as of Monterey. bootstrap.sh installs it, or I can type in the Terminal

softwareupdate --install-rosetta --agree-to-license

items.title: Shell
items.text: zsh is the default shell in macOS as of Catalina.

items.title: Extensions
items.text:
bootstrap.sh installs these and turns them on with omz, which edits ~/.zshrc for you:

  • Oh My Zsh
  • zsh-autoswitch-virtualenv
    • omz plugin enable autoswitch_virtualenv
  • spaceship-prompt
    • omz theme set spaceship
  • zsh-syntax-highlighting
    • Bundled with Oh My Zsh. omz plugin enable zsh-syntax-highlighting

Note

zsh-autoswitch-virtualenv and spaceship-prompt aren't bundled with Oh My Zsh. Install them into $ZSH_CUSTOM first, following the Oh My Zsh instructions in each repo (bootstrap.sh does this). Until then, omz can't find them, so omz plugin enable and omz theme set fail.

items.title: Settings for Terminal
items.text:
Terminal settings/preferences (personal choice): Ocean_Esh.terminal

bootstrap.sh imports it as the Ocean_Esh profile and makes it the default. To do it by hand,

  1. Open the Terminal, and go to Settings Profiles
  2. Hit the three dots in the bottom left corner and click Import...
  3. Select the terminal preferences file and set it as the default

items.title: Verified Git commits
items.text:
For that sweet Verified mark next to commits on GitHub, the simplest method is to generate a GPG key and associate it with your account. Start with

gpg --default-new-key-algo rsa4096 --gen-key
# Enter real name
# Enter email address associated with GitHub account
# Don't enter a passphrase unless you want to type it in every time you commit
# Enter `o` to finish

Then view the key with

gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format=long

The output will look something like

gpg: checking the trustdb
gpg: marginals needed: 3  completes needed: 1  trust model: pgp
gpg: depth: 0  valid:   1  signed:   0  trust: 0-, 0q, 0n, 0m, 0f, 1u
gpg: next trustdb check due at 2024-12-01
/Users/username/.gnupg/pubring.kbx
--------------------------------
sec   rsa4096/ABC123DEF456GHI 2022-12-02 [SC] [expires: 2024-12-01]
      JBNM4H5LJK5BKJ4BMNVTBHOI4H55P4BJ5K6L4JKL
uid                 [ultimate] Real Name <username@domain.com>

The bit after sec rsa4096/ is what we need next (ABC123DEF456GHI). To show the public key, do

gpg --armor --export ABC123DEF456GHI

which will output something like

-----BEGIN PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK-----

AMASSIVEBLOCKOFLETTERSNUMBERSANDSYMBOLS
-----END PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK-----

Remove existing keys and associate this one to your GitHub account with

git config --global --unset gpg.format
git config --global user.signingkey ABC123DEF456GHI
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

Then copy that public key we generated earlier (in its entirety), and add it to your GitHub account:

  1. Visit https://github.com/settings/gpg/new
  2. Add a title
  3. Paste the public key
  4. Hit Add GPG key

This should apply to GitHub Desktop as well, not just commits on the CLI. Just ensure you're using the same email address for your commits as entered when creating the key. Double check in Preferences Git Email.

items.title: Homebrew
items.text:
Homebrew Homebrew is an excellent, open source package manager for macOS. It's full of useful GUI programs as well as command line utilities that can be easily installed.

It should keep them up to date without requiring conscious individual checks, and should install the right versions for my architecture (i.e., Intel x64 or Apple Silicon) and OS version.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
bootstrap.sh installs Homebrew and everything in the Brewfile. To install Homebrew by hand, follow the instructions at https://brew.sh/.(1) This should also install the Xcode Command Line Tools, which are useful for software development.(2)

  1. The installer prints the line to add Homebrew to your PATH. On Apple Silicon, it's eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)" in ~/.zprofile.
  2. The manpage is at https://docs.brew.sh/Manpage, containing a bunch of useful commands like autoremove (to remove unused dependencies).

items.title: Packages
items.text:
Everything I install with Homebrew is in the Brewfile:

# CLI utilities
brew "emacs" # Not bundled with macOS since Catalina
brew "git", link: :overwrite # Newer than the version bundled with macOS
brew "gnupg" # For signing Git commits
brew "poetry" # For repos that still use Poetry
brew "pyenv" # For repos that still use pyenv
brew "tree"
brew "uv" # Default for Python installs, projects and environments
brew "wget"
brew "zsh" # Newer than the version bundled with macOS
cask "antigravity-cli"

# GUI applications
cask "1password"
cask "adobe-creative-cloud" # Lightroom and other Adobe products
cask "android-file-transfer" # Copying files to Oculus Quest
cask "ankerwork" # Webcam configuration
cask "antigravity-ide"
cask "bibdesk", args: { appdir: "/Applications/TeX" } # Managing BibTeX references
cask "blackhole-64ch" # Capturing audio output alongside a screen recording
cask "chatgpt"
cask "discord"
cask "docker-desktop"
cask "filebot" # Batch renaming. If it won't open, run `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/FileBot.app`
cask "github"
cask "google-chrome"
cask "google-drive"
cask "google-gemini" # Desktop client for Gemini's chat interface
cask "handbrake-app"
cask "jetbrains-toolbox"
cask "logi-options+"
cask "mactex-no-gui" # TeX Live, without TeXShop, LaTeXiT, etc.
cask "mimestream" # Gmail client. Requires a subscription
cask "mkvtoolnix-app" # Adding/removing audio and subtitle tracks in MKV files
cask "obsidian"
cask "plex"
cask "quicklook-video" # Thumbnails for MKV and other video formats
cask "raindropio"
cask "runescape"
cask "sidequest" # Sideloading content onto Oculus Quest
cask "steam"
cask "surfshark"
cask "tailscale-app" # Remote access to other devices, e.g., a NAS
cask "tex-live-utility", args: { appdir: "/Applications/TeX" } # Updating TeX Live packages
cask "the-unarchiver" # More versatile than the built-in archive utility
cask "thebrowsercompany-dia"
cask "todoist-app"
cask "vivid-app" # Higher display brightness. Requires a licence
cask "vlc"
cask "warp" # A nicer, modern terminal with agentic capabilities and settings sync
cask "whatsapp"

Install or update them all with

brew bundle install --file ~/GitHub/macOS-setup/Brewfile

To add a package, add it to the Brewfile rather than running brew install, so it's installed on every Mac. brew bundle cleanup --file ~/GitHub/macOS-setup/Brewfile lists anything installed that isn't in the Brewfile (add --force to uninstall them).

brew lines install formulae (command line tools), and cask lines install GUI applications into the Applications folder. Some programs come as both, e.g., handbrake is the command line version and handbrake-app is the GUI.

For any issues with opening these programs, see https://support.apple.com/en-gb/guide/mac-help/mh40616/mac.

items.title: Updating
items.text:
Upgrade Homebrew packages with

brew upgrade

Casks with auto-update utilities (like a lot of GUI applications) may also be updated here.

items.title: Viewing
items.text:
Check everything that's installed with

brew list

Check only top-level formulae with

brew leaves

Add the -r option for formulae that were explicitly installed, or -p for formulae installed as a dependency of a cask.

Check which formulae and casks are using a specific dependency with

brew uses --installed --recursive <dependency>

items.title: Cleanup and uninstalling
items.text:
Homebrew should run a cleanup of caches and old files every so often. For manual scrubbing, run

brew cleanup -s --prune all

Uninstall a formula/cask with

brew uninstall <formula/cask>

Add the --zap option to remove all associated files.

Uninstall unused dependencies of formulae/casks with

brew autoremove

items.title: VS Code
items.text:
In Visual Studio Code, the settings.json file can be edited to override some default commands. My current list of installed extensions are

  • bibtexLanguage
  • GitLens
  • LaTeX Workshop
  • markdownlint
  • Project Dashboard
  • Pylance
  • Python
  • Rainbow CSV
  • Remote - SSH
  • Remote - SSH: Editing Configuration Files
  • Spell Right
  • vscode-icons

and the settings file is vscode_settings.json. Even though it should be backed up to my GitHub account (@eshwen), a cold copy could be handy. Make sure the Python path reflects whatever version I have installed. It can be switched on-the-fly in any case.

items.title: TeX Live
items.text:
TeX Live is installed with the mactex-no-gui cask in the Brewfile. It's the full MacTeX distribution without the GUI applications like TeXShop and LaTeXiT, which I don't need since VS Code is way better. The two GUI applications I do use, BibDesk (for managing BibTeX references) and TeX Live Utility (for updating TeX Live packages), are separate casks in the Brewfile, so Homebrew keeps them up to date. They're installed into /Applications/TeX.

MacTeX/TeX Live installs as root (possibly to avoid large installs and conflicts for multiple users). So if avoiding TeX Live Utility to update packages, I can go via the command line with sudo privileges. Check for outdated packages with

sudo tlmgr update --list

Update the package manager itself with

sudo tlmgr update --self

and then update the packages with

sudo tlmgr update --all

items.title: Garamond Expert
items.text:
My favourite font is Garamond Expert with New TX Math (the LaTeX package garamondx - see here). As well as being visually appealing, it supports bold, italic, and small cap styles that other Garamond variants do not. If compiling a LaTeX document on Overleaf, this should already be installed. However, it is not bundled with TeX Live due to licensing. bootstrap.sh installs it, along with the other non-free fonts. To do it by hand, follow the instructions at http://tug.org/fonts/getnonfreefonts/:

curl --remote-name https://www.tug.org/fonts/getnonfreefonts/install-getnonfreefonts
sudo texlua install-getnonfreefonts
sudo getnonfreefonts --sys -a

If the above doesn't work (sometimes the microtype package fails to map things properly), also try

updmap-sys

Do not run getnonfreefonts with --user, or updmap-user, for the reasons outlined in https://tex.stackexchange.com/a/255711.

items.title: Programs
items.text: Here you can find a list of programs that may be useful for Mac users. The list is not exhaustive, but it's a good starting point for setting up a new machine.

items.title: Fonts
items.text: There are some nice fonts I've found over the years in the fonts directory. bootstrap.sh copies them to ~/Library/Fonts. To install them by hand, highlight them all in the Finder and double click.

items.title: Non-Homebrew
items.text:
While the aim is to install everything with Homebrew, not all programs are available. These include

  • Fujifilm X RAW Studio
  • Glow
  • OpenEmu (its Homebrew cask is disabled because it fails Gatekeeper checks)
  • Viltrox Lens

items.title: Python
items.text: Python is not bundled with macOS as of v13.

items.title: uv
items.text:
uv manages Python installs, virtual environments, dependencies and CLI tools in one place, so it's the default for any new project. pyenv and Poetry are still installed with Homebrew for repos that use them. Once it's been installed with Homebrew, install a recent version of Python with

uv python install <version>

Multiple installations are supported. List the installed and available versions with

uv python list

items.title: Projects
items.text:
Start a new project, add dependencies, and run code in its environment with

uv init
uv add <package>
uv run <command>

uv sync installs everything in uv.lock into .venv, e.g., after cloning a repo.

items.title: Tools
items.text:
Install Python CLI tools into their own isolated environments with

uv tool install <package>

or run one without installing it with uvx <package>.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text: See https://github.com/eshwen/ds-python-boilerplate for a list of common Python dependencies for data science.
